storyboard.claim: Humbert treats Charlotte with relentless aristocratic contempt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing aloof in Charlotte's parlor, looking down his nose at her — his posture radiates disdain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Context said he arrived at 342 Lawn Street; now we see how he treats his hostess.
storyboard.addedInformation: His cold, dismissive stance makes visible the contempt the narration describes.

storyboard.claim: Humbert calls Charlotte's house a 'white frame horror' and mocks everything about her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The home icon — the literal house he is describing and despising. Humbert points at the room, sneering at her domestic world.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues from his condescension: now specific insults about her house.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style: the narrators flag this as Humbert's cruel framing, not truth. Home icon reads as the literal house being mocked.

storyboard.claim: Humbert mocks Charlotte's appearance, her French, her book club, her furniture — everything.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing dismissively while Charlotte holds a book (her book club). His contemptuous face says it all.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Escalation: from the house to every detail of her life.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte holding the book club book grounds the mockery in something concrete the viewer can see.

storyboard.claim: Nabokov weaponizes our reactions against us through Humbert's mockery of consumerism.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov as the architect, pointing — directing the reader's reaction like a stage director.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pulls back from Humbert's mockery to the author's design behind it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shifting to Nabokov shows the manipulation is structural, not accidental.

storyboard.claim: On the surface, the Charlotte scenes read like brilliant screwball comedy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert and Charlotte on a stage — the comedy is a performance. He stands coolly, she gestures beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After naming Nabokov's weapon: here is how it feels to the reader — comedy.
storyboard.addedInformation: The stage set signals this is a performance, not reality.

storyboard.claim: Humbert plays the cynical European, Charlotte the desperate widow, and we laugh along.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert with a smug grin, Charlotte with a desperate forced smile — both performing their roles in the comedy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The comedy in action: the two roles that make us laugh.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: both smiling reads as agreement, but the narration says WE laugh — the complicity is the reader's, not theirs.

storyboard.claim: Charlotte writes Humbert an intensely dramatic letter demanding he leave or marry her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte holding the letter — her desperate bid. Her worried, yearning face shows the stakes she feels.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specific example of the comedy: her clumsy attempt to seduce him.
storyboard.addedInformation: The letter in her hands makes the drama tangible.

storyboard.claim: Her letter swings wildly between telling him to leave and declaring her love.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte alone clutching her letter, face torn between desperation and hope.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms into the letter's content: the melodramatic ultimatum.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing her alone emphasizes her vulnerability — she has no one else to turn to.

storyboard.claim: Humbert coldly calculates how to use Charlotte's desperation to gain permanent access to Dolores.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The puppeteer icon — Humbert is literally manipulating Charlotte's love to control the situation. He thinks coldly while she stands hopeful beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The comedy flips: her desperate love letter is his strategic opportunity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puppeteer reads as one person controlling others — exactly what Humbert does with her emotions.

storyboard.claim: The laughter stops when you realize what the comedy is hiding.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mask icon — the comedy itself was a mask over cruelty. Humbert stands on a stage, the performance exposed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After laughing with him: the moment of recognition that we were tricked.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask reads as a false public face — the comedy IS the false face concealing predation.

storyboard.claim: Charlotte is not a cartoon character — she is a profoundly lonely woman.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte sitting alone in her parlor, looking sad — the real person behind the comedy caricature.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After unmasking the comedy: now see the real Charlotte underneath.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing her alone and sad reframes every scene we laughed at.

storyboard.claim: Humbert marries Charlotte solely to gain access to her 12-year-old daughter.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing cold and calculating beside Charlotte, who looks at him with genuine love — the asymmetry is the horror.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The real motive behind the marriage, after seeing Charlotte's loneliness.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte's loving expression contrasted with Humbert's cold neutrality shows the one-sided exploitation.

storyboard.claim: The comedy is moral anesthesia — Nabokov makes Humbert charming to make us complicit in cruelty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov pointing out the mechanism he built — the author as architect of the reader's complicity.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the technique: after seeing what the comedy hid, here is the clinical term.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's exact phrase, a key concept in the analysis.

storyboard.claim: Humbert pivots from mocking Charlotte to plotting her murder at Hourglass Lake.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert thinking coldly at the shore while Charlotte stands nearby, unaware — the lake setting grounds the scene.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After moral anesthesia: the concrete example of how quickly comedy turns to murder.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte's happy unawareness next to his cold plotting face shows the lethal asymmetry.

storyboard.claim: Swimming together, Humbert vividly imagines drowning Charlotte.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Water icon — the drowning IS the subject. Humbert reaches toward Charlotte at the shore, his face cold and calculating.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From plotting in general to the specific method: drowning in this lake.
storyboard.addedInformation: His reaching action toward her makes the murder fantasy visible. Water reads literally as water — they are in a lake.

storyboard.claim: Humbert describes the exact mechanics: grab her ankle, dive with his 'captive corpse.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert reaching toward Charlotte — the chilling direct quote made visible through his predatory posture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the drowning fantasy with Humbert's own clinical language.
storyboard.addedInformation: His exact phrase 'captive corpse' — she is already dead in his mind.

storyboard.claim: He calculates every logistic — notices a policeman and plumber in the distance, too far to see.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert alone at the shore, thinking — scanning the distance, calculating witnesses and angles like a tactician.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the drowning method to the logistics: witnesses, distances, alibis.
storyboard.addedInformation: Showing him alone and thinking emphasizes the cold solitary calculation.

storyboard.claim: He calculates the witnesses are far enough not to see the murder but close enough to hear him yell for help after.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing into the distance — measuring the exact distance to potential witnesses for his alibi.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The final calculation: the alibi. Far enough to miss the act, close enough for the performance.
storyboard.addedInformation: His pointing makes the tactical measurement visible.

storyboard.claim: He decides not to drown her — but NOT out of conscience or empathy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing still, face blank and unmoved — no sign of moral feeling, no warmth, no regret.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After all that planning: why he stops. The answer is NOT what you hope.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style: the narrators reject the idea he has a conscience. His blank expression stages the absence of feeling.

storyboard.claim: He stops only because he fears the logistics of getting away with it — pure self-preservation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert looking worried for the first time — but worried about himself, not about her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After rejecting conscience: the real reason. Fear of consequences, not morality.
storyboard.addedInformation: His worried face is about himself, not his victim — the only time his composure breaks is over logistics.

storyboard.claim: Humbert addresses the jury: 'We are not sex fiends' — performing innocence in a legal frame.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Law icon — he is literally addressing a jury. Humbert talks to an invisible courtroom, performing his defense.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the private calculation to the public defense: he pivots to the jury.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style: the narrators flatly reject this self-description. Law icon reads as courtroom/legal — he IS making a legal argument.

storyboard.claim: He calls himself an 'unhappy, mild, dog-eyed gentleman' — using self-pity as armor.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Shield icon — his words are literal protection against judgment. Humbert performs sadness for the jury.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues his courtroom defense: from denial to self-pity.
storyboard.addedInformation: His sad expression is performed, not felt (the narrators just showed he has no conscience). Shield reads as protection — his rhetoric IS his shield.

storyboard.claim: He invokes his identity as a poet — 'Poets never kill' — the aesthetic defense again.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding a book (his literary identity) while speaking to the jury — wielding art as alibi.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Third layer of defense: from denial to pity to the aesthetic claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike: the narrators call this out as the recurring 'aesthetic defense.' The book in his hand IS his weapon.

storyboard.claim: He claims gentleness while having just spent five pages planning murder — the mask of sensitivity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains icon — constraint and control. Humbert speaks with cold neutral expression, the meticulous planner.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The narrators' counter-punch: you just READ the murder plan, and now he says 'poets never kill.'
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains read as deliberate control/planning — five pages of calculated murder, not shocked reaction.

storyboard.claim: Dark fate intervenes: Charlotte discovers Humbert's secret diary and learns the truth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte holding the diary (book), her face in shock — the moment of discovery that shatters everything.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the failed murder: fate provides another path — the diary.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her surprise is genuine horror: she realizes the man she loves is a monster.

storyboard.claim: Charlotte flees the house in hysterics to mail letters exposing Humbert to the town.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte rushing into the street clutching letters, her face terrified — fleeing to save her daughter.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From discovery to action: she tries to expose him and protect Dolores.
storyboard.addedInformation: The letter in her hand shows her plan — to expose him. Walking action stands for running (the most urgent action available).

storyboard.claim: Charlotte is violently struck and killed by a car.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Crash icon — the literal car collision. Charlotte in the street at the moment of impact.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: She never mails the letters. The exposure attempt ends in sudden death.
storyboard.addedInformation: Crash reads as a collision — exactly what happens. Her surprised face is the last instant.

storyboard.claim: Humbert does not describe the tragedy of a life lost — he reduces her physical destruction to aesthetics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing at the scene, face completely blank — no grief, no horror, just cold observation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the crash: not his reaction to her death, but how he DESCRIBES it.
storyboard.addedInformation: His blank neutrality at a death scene is the visual — the absence of feeling IS the point.

storyboard.claim: He turns her death into pure poetic alliteration — a literary exercise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Notes icon — he is literally writing. Humbert holds his manuscript, turning death into prose.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From reducing her to... THIS: words on a page. Notes = the confession manuscript.
storyboard.addedInformation: Notes reads as writing/documents — he IS treating her death as writing material. The abstract set removes all human context.

storyboard.claim: Bone, brains, bronze hair, blood — to him it is just alliteration, a string of B sounds.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking clinically, face unmoved — reciting her destruction as if reading poetry aloud.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific example of the aestheticization: the alliterative list.
storyboard.addedInformation: His neutral talking pose while describing death drives home the dehumanization.

storyboard.claim: To Humbert, Charlotte was never a person — merely an obstacle on his path to Dolores.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walking toward Dolores — Charlotte gone, the obstacle removed, his path clear.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After reducing her death to sound: the final erasure — she was never real to him.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dolores on screen for the first time in this sequence reveals what all of this was always about.

storyboard.claim: The screwball comedy abruptly ends and the true horror of the novel begins.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow diagram: Obstacle removed -> Comedy ends -> Horror begins. Humbert walks forward into the next phase.
storyboard.onScreenText: Obstacle Removed → Comedy Ends → Horror Begins
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Structural pivot: the three-step transition from comedy to horror.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram makes the novel's structural shift visible — this is the hinge of the entire book.

storyboard.claim: With Charlotte eliminated, Humbert now has total unquestioned control over Dolores.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Puppeteer icon — Humbert controlling Dolores completely. He stands over her, idle and in command.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the structural pivot: the new reality. No one stands between them now.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puppeteer reads as one person controlling others — exactly the dynamic. Dolores's worried face shows she is trapped.

storyboard.claim: Humbert picks up Dolores from camp — she does not yet know her mother is dead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walking with Dolores, his face neutral and composed; she does not know what has happened.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From total control to the first action: collecting his captive.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her ignorance is the horror — she walks beside the man who engineered (or at least benefited from) her mother's death.

storyboard.claim: Humbert initiates a year-long cross-country drive — August 1947 to August 1948.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Road icon — the literal cross-country journey. Humbert and Dolores on the highway, the road stretching ahead.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From picking her up to the journey: the geographic scope of the captivity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Road reads as a road/journey — the drive IS the subject.

storyboard.claim: On the surface, Humbert writes this section like a classic expansive American road adventure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert and Dolores on the open highway — the surface appearance of a grand journey.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the year-long drive: how Humbert frames it — as freedom and adventure.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: without the coming undercut (beat 118) this could read as genuinely positive, but the neutral expressions hint something is off.

storyboard.claim: They visit cabins, drive through sagebrush wilderness, cross mountain passes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert and Dolores sitting together on the highway — the postcard version of their journey.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specific details of the surface adventure: the picturesque travelogue.
storyboard.addedInformation: Their sitting together looks peaceful — the irony is that this peace is captivity.

storyboard.claim: Neon signs, roadside diners, motor courts — it sounds incredibly expansive and free.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert and Dolores on the highway — the narrator's question hangs: 'doesn't it?'
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The surface reading reaches its peak before the undercut.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style: the narrators are about to reject this framing — it is NOT free. The strike signals the irony before the reveal.

storyboard.claim: In reality, the great American road trip is a kidnapping in perpetual motion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains icon — Dolores is imprisoned. She sits sad on the highway, trapped beside Humbert.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The undercut: 'expansive and free' was a lie. This is captivity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains reads as bound, imprisoned — Dolores IS a captive. Dolores listed first in cast because she is the subject now, not Humbert.

storyboard.claim: Nabokov uses America's massive scale to show an abused child can be completely invisible in plain sight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores sitting small and sad on the vast highway, Humbert beside her — the scale dwarfs her, she disappears into the landscape.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From kidnapping to its mechanism: the continent itself hides her.
storyboard.addedInformation: The highway set emphasizes the massive, empty American geography that makes her invisible. Context-after confirms: 'the movement itself becomes the cage.'
